sh=lambda x: x.mean()/x.std()*np.sqrt(252)
def evalsplit(a,b,c):
    A=R[a:b]; B=R[b:c]
    s=np.array([sh(A[:,i]) for i in range(423)])
    out={}
    for k in [10,20,50,100,423]:
        ix=np.argsort(-np.abs(s))[:k]; w=np.sign(s[ix])
        out[k]=round(sh(B[:,ix]@w),2)
    # inverse-vol sign-weighted by sharpe
    w=s/A.std(0); out['tilt']=round(sh(B@w),2)
    return out
y=T//30

    print(st, evalsplit(0,st*y,min(T,(st+5)*y)))

content.text: I ran one validation backtest and it came back FAIL. I'm going to submit this portfolio as it stands rather than keep searching for a PASS.

I submitted an equal-weight portfolio of 94 signals: long all 47 one-month industry momentum signals (`tsmom_*_21`) and short all 47 slow moving-average signals (`ma_*_50_200`), i.e. betting on short-term industry momentum and long-term reversal. It has a training Sharpe of 0.37 (1970–1999) and was positive in 5 of 6 five-year blocks, but its one validation backtest (2000–2012) came back **FAIL**.

I used only 1 of the 200 backtests on purpose. Within the training data, almost nothing held up out of sample: in-sample and out-of-sample Sharpe ratios correlated at about 0.16, and picking the top signals in walk-forward tests mostly lost money. Running a large search against the validation verdict would almost certainly produce a PASS by chance alone. That PASS would carry no information about how the portfolio does in 2000–2012, and it would likely mean a lower true validation Sharpe, not a higher one. So I fixed the portfolio in advance from training data only and submitted it despite the FAIL. The honest conclusion is that these signals show no reliable alpha.
